title: Estimating the risk of recession in the US
gist: FRED added a new monthly US recession-probability dataset from RecessionRisk.com (Furno and Giannone), which combines the manufacturing PMI and the ECB's Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress; the August 2026 reading was just 0.08%, and while spikes broadly track actual NBER recessions, some past spikes (October 1998, March 2023) did not turn into recessions.

themes.theme: The new dataset and its current reading

insights.claim: FRED added a monthly probability-of-US-recession dataset from RecessionRisk.com, developed by economists Francesco Furno and Domenico Giannone, with the August 2026 reading at just 0.08%, available on the first business day after the reference month closes.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A 0.08% recession probability for August 2026 is an extremely low reading, and the near-real-time monthly availability (first business day after month-end) makes this a fast, freely available macro indicator worth tracking as a low-lag substitute for slower-moving recession signals.
insights.quote: The latest data, for August 2026, show that probability was 0.08%.

themes.theme: Methodology: combining growth and financial-stress signals

insights.claim: The recession probability is calculated from a statistical model combining two indicators: the ISM Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for manufacturing, and the ECB's Composite Indicator of Systemic Stress (CISS), which tracks stress across bond, equity, money, foreign exchange, and financial intermediary markets.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A two-input model (one real-economy survey, one cross-market financial-stress index) gives a simple, replicable framework for anyone wanting to build their own quick recession-risk gauge rather than relying on more opaque proprietary models.
insights.quote: The probability estimates are calculated using a statistical model that combines two indicators. The first measures broad economic conditions, and the second measures financial market stress

themes.theme: Track record: good overlap with NBER dating, but false positives exist

insights.claim: The timing of spikes in the RecessionRisk.com probability estimate broadly coincides with NBER-dated turning points into actual recessions, but several past spikes — such as around October 1998 and March 2023 — did not develop into actual recessions.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The documented false-positive history (1998, 2023) is an important caveat: a future spike in this indicator should be treated as a raised-risk signal to monitor, not a confirmed recession call, given its track record of occasional false alarms.
insights.quote: several probability spikes, such as the ones around October 1998 and March 2023, did not develop into actual recessions
